title: Risk of Developing Subsequent Primary Colorectal Cancers Among Non-Colorectal Cancer Survivors: Implications for Prevention and Screening

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Risk of Developing Subsequent Primary Colorectal Cancers Among Non-Colorectal Cancer Survivors: Implications for Prevention and Screening》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · ijc70690-sec-0001-p1】Improvements in early cancer detection and treatment approaches have shifted several common types of cancer from acute diseases with high mortality to chronic conditions requiring long‐term management [1]. There are now twice as many long‐term cancer survivors as there were 20 years ago with similar increases expected over the next 20 years based on current projections [2, 3]. One unique challenge for cancer survivors is that they carry a higher risk of developing a new or “subsequent primary cancer” compared to the cancer‐free population developing a first cancer [4]. However, little is known about whether specific survivorship groups are most clinically important and whether the absolute risks are high enough to warrant intervention. Approximately 15%–25% of cancer survivors will develop a subsequent primary cancer during their lifetime, thus contributing significantly to morbidity, mortality, and healthcare utilization [4, 5, 6].

【Introduction · ijc70690-sec-0001-p2】Cancer survivors are at a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer (CRC) than the general population and CRC is one of the most common subsequent primary cancer sites to occur among cancer survivors [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. CRC screening has dual benefits because it can decrease mortality through early detection and can also reduce incidence through the removal of precancerous polyps. CRC incidence is declining faster than any other cancer in Canada and this decline is largely attributed to the implementation of organized CRC screening programs across Canada [10]. Despite cancer survivors being at an elevated risk for CRC, current guidelines typically recommend adult cancer survivors undergo CRC screening that is similar to the general population, with the exception of CRC survivors or those who received abdominal/pelvic/spinal/total body radiation therapy as a child/young adult [11, 12].

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Risk of Developing Subsequent Primary Colorectal Cancers Among Non-Colorectal Cancer Survivors: Implications for Prevention and Screening》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Study Design and Population · ijc70690-sec-0003-p1】We conducted a population‐based retrospective cohort study of adult (≥ 18 years of age at diagnosis) survivors of a cancer diagnosis recorded in the Alberta Cancer Registry from January 1, 2000, to July 1, 2021 who survived at least 180 days following diagnosis. The 180‐day cut‐off was selected to align with the definition of metachronous (develops subsequently) primary cancer [14]. Patients were followed from 180 days after diagnosis until December 31, 2021 (administrative censoring), death from any cause, or the diagnosis of a colorectal adenocarcinoma. Survivors of CRC were excluded given enhanced monitoring for disease recurrence and screening for CRC. However, a secondary analysis among CRC survivors was conducted to provide a comparison to survivors of non‐CRC sites.

【Study Design and Population · ijc70690-sec-0003-p3】Treatment information on cancer survivors was acquired via deterministic linkage to the ARIA‐MO (Medical Oncology) database. ARIA‐MO consists of electronic medical records for all 17 provincial cancer centers (2 tertiary, 4 regional, and 11 community centers) and contains data related to patient care including information on surgery, systemic therapies, and radiation therapy. Information on neighborhood‐level socioeconomic status (median income and urban/rural residence) was obtained using census information from Statistics Canada, linked based on the first three digits of patients' residential postal code. Patients' medical history and comorbidities around first primary cancer diagnosis (from 6 months prior to 6 months after) were assessed using information from provincial administrative data sources, including Physician Billing Claims, the Discharge Abstract Database, and the National Ambulatory Care Reporting System. Patients' body mass index (BMI) was calculated based on height and weight recorded during cancer‐related clinical visits within 6 months prior to 2 years after first primary cancer diagnosis; when multiple time points were available, the weight recorded closest to diagnosis was used.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Risk of Developing Subsequent Primary Colorectal Cancers Among Non-Colorectal Cancer Survivors: Implications for Prevention and Screening》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Results · ijc70690-sec-0005-p4】A sensitivity analysis including carcinoid tumors in addition to adenocarcinomas found that SIRs and IRDs were slightly higher, compared to analysis of adenocarcinomas alone (Figure S2). In this analysis, lung cancer survivors were additionally identified as being at a significantly elevated risk of SPCRC, while kidney and NHL survivors had increased risk approaching statistical significance. Regarding inclusion of patients with metastatic disease, only 78 SPCRC cases occurred among metastatic cancer survivors and no site‐specific metastatic groups had elevated risk compared to the cancer‐free population. When combining first primary cancer sites by common etiology with CRC (obesity, alcohol, smoking), first primary cancers that shared a risk factor with CRC had a slightly higher risk (SIR: 1.31 [1.22–1.40]) than those without smoking‐ alcohol‐, or obesity‐related etiology (SIR: 1.23 [1.15–1.30]), although the risk remained significantly elevated compared to the cancer‐free population.

【Results · ijc70690-sec-0005-p8】Regarding the risk of SPCRC across the length of survivorship (Figure S5; Table S6), IRDs and SIRs were the lowest during 6‐months to 5‐years after first primary cancer diagnosis (IRD: 24.1 [14.2–34.6] per 100,000 person‐years; SIR: 1.20 [1.12–1.28]). The risks were steadily elevated over the remaining periods with IRDs of 44.9, 39.6, and 41.9, and SIRs of 1.34, 1.29, and 1.32 during periods 5–10 years, 10–15 years, and 15+ years after first primary cancer diagnosis, respectively. The risk of late stage SPCRC was elevated across all survivorship age groups, with statistically significant increased risk for those aged 50+ (Figure S6); similarly, the risk of late stage SPCRC was elevated across all survivorship periods (Figure S7). Finally, across subsites, the highest risk for late stage SPCRC was found in the proximal colon (Figure S8).
